title: Executive Summary
content:
Gaza's rehabilitation crisis is not a device shortage alone; it is the collapse of an entire continuum of care for tens of thousands of persons with disabilities, amputees above all, alongside survivors of traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury. This proposal responds with a comprehensive, integrated, and field-proven service delivery intervention that brings rehabilitation to where people are a minimum of three fixed rehabilitation points, six mobile teams, and one central prosthetics center, wrapping every beneficiary in physical rehabilitation, mental health and psychosocial support, surgical intervention, nutrition and food voucher assistance, and pathways to livelihood and education reintegration.
Gaza's rehabilitation system is facing a critical and unprecedented humanitarian emergency. The prolonged conflict, with its widespread use of explosive munitions, blast injuries, and shrapnel trauma in one of the world's most densely populated urban environments, has produced a scale of complex disability with no modern parallel in humanitarian response history. By mid-2026, more than 6,500 people in Gaza are living with war-related amputations, while an estimated 41,844 individuals, approximately 1.9% of Gaza's pre-conflict population, require sustained, long-term rehabilitation services [1, 2]. Beyond limb loss, the same blast mechanisms have produced substantial caseloads of traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI), conditions that demand long-duration, multidisciplinary rehabilitation and lifelong assistive support. At the same time, Gaza's rehabilitation infrastructure has been devastated: facilities destroyed, practitioners displaced or lost, and supply chains for prosthetic components and assistive devices severely disrupted [3, 4].
Fragmented, single-service responses cannot break this cycle. RHS's own operational data from Gaza (2025) documents prosthetic abandonment rates exceeding 80% in fragmented, device-only humanitarian programs, consistent with the broader humanitarian rehabilitation literature [15]. Devices distributed without qualified fitting, rehabilitation, psychosocial support, and nutritional care are devices abandoned; and rehabilitation delivered only from fixed sites never reaches the majority of persons with disabilities who cannot travel to it.
To address this gap, Restoring Hope Society (RHS) proposes an integrated rehabilitation and prosthetics program for persons with disabilities in Gaza, with a special focus on amputees, and encompassing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury cases, delivered through a service network of a minimum of three fixed rehabilitation points, six mobile teams reaching beneficiaries in shelters, camps, and hard-to-reach areas, and one central, fully equipped prosthetics center providing casting, fabrication, fitting, and gait training. Every case is identified, assessed, and managed through RHS's structured, data collection and case management workflow, producing an individually tailored service package for each beneficiary and their family.
Every beneficiary receives a full integrated holistic care package comprising physical rehabilitation, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), surgical intervention where clinically required, nutritional support, and food vouchers for households in acute food insecurity. Beyond clinical recovery, the program invests in reintegration: 20% of beneficiaries will receive livelihood support, grounded in a rapid market assessment to ensure the sustainability of their income-generating projects, followed up by the RHS team, and supported by RHS's communication and advocacy team in developing the marketing plans for their projects, while children are reintegrated into education through RHS's collaboration with International NGOs, embedding specialized rehabilitation and MHPSS points within temporary learning spaces.
Underpinning the clinical program is a logistics and supply capability few actors in Gaza can match: RHS operates warehouses in both Gaza and Amman; works through WHO, WFP, international NGOs, and the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization (JHCO) to move goods into Gaza; and delivered a shipment of approximately 800 prosthetics on 15 June 2026, including components and equipment for two partner organizations working in prosthetics in Gaza, with a further prosthetics shipment planned on bi-monthly basis to bring in prosthetics and raw materials for all actors, ensuring continuity of services across all workshops and locations.
It is important to understand precisely what RHS means by the phrase 'integrated care' and why it appears not as a single section but as a thread running through every dimension of this document, the rationale, the objectives, the beneficiary pathway, the service network design, the staffing structure, the monitoring framework, and the communication strategy. RHS does not regard physical rehabilitation, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), nutritional assistance, food vouchers, transport, and case management as optional add-ons that improve an already-complete prosthetic or rehabilitation service. RHS regards them as essential parts of what rehabilitation is. A device fitted, or a course of therapy delivered, without these services is, in RHS's clinical and organizational judgment, an incomplete intervention regardless of its technical quality, and RHS's own field data and the wider humanitarian rehabilitation literature confirm that incomplete interventions of this kind fail at rates exceeding 80% [15, 4]. For that reason, this proposal presents the fixed rehabilitation points, the mobile teams, the central prosthetics center, and the full integrated care, livelihood, and education reintegration pathway as a single project with a single budget, a single staffing structure, and a single management line, not as a rehabilitation project accompanied by separately funded companion initiatives.

title: Problem Statement
content:
## The Scale of Amputation Crisis in Gaza
The conflict in Gaza has produced a physical injury burden of exceptional scale and complexity. The combination of explosive munitions, aerial bombardment, blast trauma, and secondary fragmentation injuries has generated patterns of traumatic amputation rarely seen outside wartime, compounded by the near-total collapse of Gaza trauma surgical and post-operative care systems. As of mid-2026, an estimated 6,500 or more people in Gaza are living with war-related amputations [1, 4]. This figure continues to grow: the Gaza Ministry of Health documents an average of 15 children per day acquiring a lifelong disability during the conflict period, a rate that, if sustained, will add thousands of new rehabilitation cases annually for years to come [11, 12].
The typology of injuries presenting in Gaza is disproportionately severe. High-level amputations, transfemoral (above-knee), hip disarticulation, and bilateral lower-limb cases constitute a significantly higher share of the caseload than in peacetime settings, reflecting the nature of explosive injury trauma. These cases require the highest levels of prosthetic clinical skill, the most complex socket designs, the most sophisticated componentry, and the most intensive rehabilitation. Alongside limb loss, blast trauma and structural collapse have produced significant caseloads of traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI), conditions requiring specialized, long-duration neurorehabilitation, assistive devices and mobility aids, caregiver training, and sustained psychosocial support. Beyond amputees, an estimated 41,844 individuals, approximately 1.9% of Gaza's pre-conflict population of 2.2 million, require sustained, long-term rehabilitation services encompassing prosthetics, orthotics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and psychological support [1, 2].
The physical infrastructure supporting rehabilitation has been devastated. Multiple rehabilitation centers, physiotherapy departments, and medical facilities have been damaged or destroyed. Supply chains for prosthetic components, lamination resins, thermoplastics, and specialist workshop materials were already fragile before the conflict and are now severely disrupted, with repeated import restrictions and port closures creating acute and unpredictable material shortages [4]. International humanitarian organizations, including the ICRC, Médecins Sans Frontières, and WHO-supported facilities, have maintained partial service delivery, but their combined capacity represents only a fraction of what is required to meet the scale of need [17].

## Rehabilitation Workforce Deficit: A Structural Crisis
Gaza's prosthetics and orthotics workforce deficit represents perhaps the most severe practitioner shortage of any humanitarian context globally. As of mid-2026, only eight Certified Prosthetist-Orthotists (CPOs) are operational across the entirety of Gaza, serving a population of more than 6,500 amputees and a broader rehabilitation caseload approaching 42,000 [3, 4]. The resulting practitioner-to-patient ratio of approximately 1:625 stands at 25 times below the minimum international benchmark of one qualified practitioner per 25 to 30 patients in a high-caseload setting, a standard established by the International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO) and the World Health Organization for conflict-affected and low-resource environments [3, 5].
This is not a capacity gap: it is a structural collapse. Even prior to the current conflict, Gaza's rehabilitation workforce was severely undersized relative to the territory's historical injury burden from previous conflicts and the long-term consequences of Gaza's economic isolation. The current emergency has eliminated much of what existed, caused the displacement or loss of several of the most experienced practitioners, and left tens of thousands of persons with disabilities — amputees, TBI and SCI survivors — with no realistic route to care [4]. A workforce deficit of this depth cannot be reversed in the near term. What it demands now is that the qualified clinical capacity that does exist be deployed with maximum efficiency and reach: through fixed rehabilitation points located where caseloads concentrate, mobile teams that carry services to beneficiaries who cannot travel, and a central prosthetics center in which scarce P&O expertise, equipment, and materials are concentrated to serve the entire Strip.
The consequences of this workforce gap are documented and severe. In the absence of qualified practitioners, patients are denied access to evidence-based assessment, anatomically accurate socket design, and proper prosthetic alignment, producing devices that cause skin breakdown, wound infection,gait disorders, chronic pain, and secondary musculoskeletal disability [15, 16]. The psychological consequences of poorly fitted or unusable prosthetics in a population already experiencing severe conflict-related trauma are profound, contributing to abandonment of devices, withdrawal from rehabilitation programs, and the perpetuation of long-term disability [16]. RHS's own operational data from Gaza (2025) shows prosthetic abandonment rates exceeding 80% in programs that provide devices without concurrent qualified fitting, physiotherapy, psychological support, and nutritional care [4].

## Regional and Comparative Context
The rehabilitation workforce crisis in Gaza is part of a broader regional pattern, but Gaza represents the most extreme documented case. In Syria, similar workforce deficits, estimated at 12 qualified rehabilitation professionals per 100,000 displaced persons requiring rehabilitation, have driven comparable abandonment rates and long-term disability burdens [6]. In Sudan's conflict-affected regions, where an estimated 250,000 people require prosthetic and orthotic services, the practitioner coverage rate falls to below 2% of need [7]. In the West Bank, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics documents a severe chronic shortage of allied health professionals across all rehabilitation specialties [8]. In Yemen, UNICEF estimates that fewer than 15% of children requiring rehabilitation services can access any form of appropriate care [9]. Across these contexts, the evidence consistently demonstrates that device provision without trained practitioners produces outcomes indistinguishable from no intervention at all [17, 20].
Gaza's situation is further distinguished by the extreme constraints on movement and access that separate persons with disabilities from the services that survive. Displacement is repeated and unpredictable; transport is scarce, costly, and often physically impossible for wheelchair users and recent amputees; and the geographic distribution of surviving services no longer corresponds to where the affected population actually lives. Any credible response must therefore be built for outreach: services must be decentralized across multiple fixed points, carried into shelters and camps by mobile teams, and coordinated through a robust case-management system that follows the beneficiary wherever they are displaced [4].

## Nutrition, Mental Health, and Multidimensional Vulnerability of Gaza’s Rehabilitation Population
The individuals who require prosthetic and rehabilitation services in Gaza are not only living with physical disability: they are navigating an extraordinarily complex multidimensional vulnerability. Ninety percent of children under two years of age in Gaza are in acute food poverty or living in extreme food insecurity [14]. Acute malnutrition at this level produces severe impairments in wound healing, in the resilience of residual limb skin to prosthetic loading, in the physiological capacity for rehabilitation, and in the immunological ability to resist post-fitting infections, all of which are direct determinants of prosthetic fitting outcomes and long-term device retention [14].
The mental health burden of Gaza's conflict-affected population is equally severe. The evidence based on conflict-related trauma, displacement, and bereavement consistently demonstrates that post-traumatic stress disorder, major depression, acute anxiety, and grief responses dramatically reduce engagement with rehabilitation services, device acceptance, motivation for gait training, and the capacity to self-manage prosthetic care [16]. Without concurrent mental health and psychosocial support delivered by trained practitioners, even technically excellent prosthetic fitting achieves outcomes substantially below therapeutic potential, and often results in complete device abandonment [15, 16].
These realities — physical disability, nutritional vulnerability, and psychological distress — are not independent problems. They constitute an interacting system of need in which intervention in one domain without the others produces minimal sustainable impact. RHS's integrated care model, described in full in Section 5.6 of this proposal, is built on this evidence base and delivers physical rehabilitation, prosthetics, MHPSS, surgical intervention, nutritional support, and food vouchers as a unified pathway for every beneficiary served under this program.

title: Rationale, Goals, and Objectives
content:
## Why Integrated Service Delivery Is the Priority, Not Device Distribution
The most frequently proposed response to disability crises in humanitarian settings is accelerated commodity distribution: importing ready-made prostheses, wheelchairs, and assistive devices and distributing them to those in need. This approach, while administratively simple, consistently produces poor outcomes when implemented in the absence of qualified assessment, fitting, rehabilitation, and follow-up. The prosthetics literature is unambiguous: device abandonment in device-only programs in conflict settings exceeds 70 to 90% within the first six months [15, 17]. Devices provided without clinical assessment and structured follow-up cause pain, skin breakdown, gait disorders, falls, and psychological harm. Their abandonment wastes donor resources, demoralizes recipients, and deepens distrust in rehabilitation services [15, 16].
In contrast, an integrated service delivery model produces compounding returns. A beneficiary who is identified early, assessed by a multidisciplinary team, prepared through pre-fitting rehabilitation and psychosocial support, fitted at a properly equipped prosthetics center, and followed through gait training to full recovery does not merely receive a device, they recover function, independence, and a pathway back into economic and social life. This is the foundational logic of this proposal: the correct entry point for Gaza's disability crisis is not the procurement of additional commodities, but the deployment of an integrated service network, a minimum of three fixed rehabilitation points, six mobile teams, and one central prosthetics center, that carries each beneficiary along the full journey from identification to reintegration, and ensures that every device provided and every therapy session delivered achieves its full therapeutic potential.

## The Urgency Window: Why Now
Several specific factors converge in mid-2026 to make this the optimal moment for an integrated rehabilitation intervention in Gaza. First, the clinical window matters: amputees who receive timely pre-fitting care, and TBI and SCI survivors who receive early rehabilitation, recover function that is permanently lost if intervention is delayed, every month without services converts treatable injury into fixed, lifelong disability. Second, RHS is already operational: its field teams, facilities, warehouses, and case-management systems are active inside Gaza, and its June 2026 shipment of approximately 800 prosthetics, with a further shipment planned for August 2026, means that materials are in place to begin fitting at scale immediately rather than after a long procurement lead time [4]. Third, the international humanitarian community's attention to Gaza's rehabilitation needs, and the corresponding donor appetite for structured, evidence-based interventions, are at a historically high level, providing funding conditions that strongly support a program of this scope.

## Alignment with international Frameworks
This proposal aligns directly with WHO's Rehabilitation 2030 initiative, which calls for urgent scaling of rehabilitation services in low- and middle-income countries and conflict settings, with specific emphasis on the integration of rehabilitation into primary and secondary health systems [5, 18]. It aligns with the ICRC's framework for rehabilitation in conflict settings, which identifies integrated, multidisciplinary service delivery, combining physical rehabilitation, prosthetics, and psychosocial support, as the minimum acceptable standard for any sustainable humanitarian rehabilitation response [17, 22]. It aligns with the Palestinian Ministry of Health's 2024–2028 Rehabilitation Strategy, which prioritizes service integration and community-based rehabilitation [23]. And it aligns with the global evidence base on disability inclusion in humanitarian response, which requires that persons with disabilities access not only health services but also livelihoods and education on an equal basis with others [13].

title: Objectives And Outcomes
content:
## Overall Goal
To restore function, dignity, and independence to conflict-affected persons with disabilities in Gaza, with a special focus on amputees, alongside traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury survivors, by delivering integrated rehabilitation, prosthetic, MHPSS, surgical, nutritional, and food security services through a network of rehabilitation points, mobile teams, and by supporting beneficiaries' economic and educational reintegration into their communities.

## Specific Objectives
This program treats service delivery infrastructure, clinical care, and social reintegration as inseparable components of a single logic of intervention. The six specific objectives below are sequenced so that each enables the next: a functioning service network (SO1) is what makes it possible to identify and manage every case through a structured, data-driven pathway (SO2), to deliver prosthetic fitting and the full integrated care package (SO3, SO4), and to carry recovered beneficiaries onward into livelihood and education reintegration (SO5, SO6). Clinical effectiveness is only achieved when every service is embedded in this full pathway, described throughout this proposal.
SO
Objective
Key Outputs
SO 1
To establish and operate an integrated rehabilitation service network fixed rehabilitation points, mobile teams, and central prosthetics center, providing equitable geographic coverage for persons with disabilities across Gaza.
>=3 rehabilitation points operational; 6 mobile teams deployed; central prosthetics center equipped and operational.
SO 2
To identify, assess, and case-manage all beneficiaries through a structured data collection and case management workflow, producing an individually tailored service package for every enrolled beneficiary and their family.
100% of beneficiaries registered through data collection; 100% receive multidisciplinary assessment and an individualized care plan.
SO 3
To provide amputees with high-quality prosthetic devices fitted, aligned, and followed up by qualified professionals at the central prosthetics center with structured pre-fitting preparation, gait training, and follow-up through full recovery.
>=80% report improved mobility; >=85% device retention at 6 months; 100% complete structured gait training and post-fitting follow-up.
SO 4
To ensure every beneficiary receives the full integrated care package, physical rehabilitation, MHPSS (including caregiver support), surgical intervention where needed, nutritional support, and food vouchers for food-insecure households — delivered as a core component of this project, alongside assistive devices distributed on the basis of assessed need.
100% enrolled in the integrated care pathway; >=80% complete minimum physiotherapy and MHPSS sessions; 100% receive nutritional assessment; food vouchers and assistive devices provided per assessed need.
SO 5
To support 20% of beneficiaries with livelihood activities — informed by a rapid market assessment to ensure the sustainability of their income-generating projects — with continued RHS follow-up and marketing support provided by the communication and advocacy team.
Rapid market assessment completed; 20% of beneficiaries launch livelihood projects; >=70% of supported projects active at 6-month follow-up.
SO 6
To reintegrate school-aged beneficiaries into education, in coordination with Save the Children International and NRC, through specialized rehabilitation and MHPSS points embedded in temporary learning spaces and MHPSS training for teachers.
100% of eligible children registered at educational points; rehabilitation and MHPSS points established in partner temporary learning spaces; teachers in target learning spaces trained on MHPSS approaches.

title: Proposed Intervention
content:
## Target Population and Selection Criteria

### Primary Beneficiaries: Persons with Disabilities, with a Special Focus on Amputees
The program targets conflict-affected persons with disabilities across the Gaza Strip, with a special focus on amputees, the largest and most clinically complex caseload, alongside survivors of traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI). Beneficiaries are identified through community outreach, Ministry of Health and partner referrals, and RHS's own field presence, and are enrolled through the structured identification and data collection workflow described in Section 5.3. Selection is conducted through a transparent, community-informed process managed by RHS in coordination with the Gaza Ministry of Health and the Health Cluster.
Selection and Prioritization Criteria:
• Persons with amputation who have not previously received a prosthetic device, or whose existing device has been destroyed, lost, or is no longer functional;
• Persons with traumatic brain injury or spinal cord injury requiring structured physical rehabilitation, assistive devices, and psychosocial support;
• Individuals at high risk of secondary disability or complications without timely intervention (assessed clinically);
• Priority representation of women, children, bilateral amputees, and high-level amputation cases;
• Medical stability for the planned interventions, as assessed by the responsible clinician, cases requiring surgical intervention first are referred to the partner hospital and re-enter the pathway after healing;
• Household vulnerability, including displacement status and food insecurity, assessed during identification to determine nutritional support and food voucher eligibility.

### Secondary Beneficiaries: Caregivers, Families, and Host Communities
Behind every person with a disability in Gaza stands a family absorbing the practical, psychological, and economic weight of care. The program therefore deliberately extends beyond the individual beneficiary: caregivers receive MHPSS sessions where needed and structured care-education sessions to learn best practices in supporting their family member's rehabilitation; households in acute food insecurity receive food vouchers; and teachers in the temporary learning spaces attended by child beneficiaries receive MHPSS training. This family-centered approach is a direct determinant of clinical outcomes: a trained, psychologically supported caregiver is the single most reliable guarantor of home-program adherence between sessions.
Caregiver and Family Support Includes:
• MHPSS sessions for caregivers, provided on the basis of assessed need;
• Physical rehabilitation care-education sessions, training caregivers in best practices for supporting the beneficiary at home;
• Nutritional education for beneficiaries and caregivers;
• Food vouchers for eligible food-insecure households, for the number of months specified in the individual care plan;
• Family inclusion in care planning, consent, and follow-up throughout the beneficiary journey.

### Direct Beneficiaries: Service Package and Total Reach
Three hundred persons with disabilities in Gaza will receive individually tailored service packages during the program period, delivered through the fixed rehabilitation points, mobile teams, and the central prosthetics center by RHS's qualified multidisciplinary field teams.
Each beneficiary's package is defined by the multidisciplinary assessment described in Section 5.3, which specifies the number of physical rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions required, nutritional support and the number of months of food voucher assistance, any need for surgical intervention, and the assistive devices required. ## Service Delivery Architecture and Implementation Model

### Overall Program Architecture
The program is structured across four integrated activity streams, each serving a distinct function, but each forming part of a single, unified project rather than separately funded activities: the service delivery network (fixed rehabilitation points, six mobile teams, and one central prosthetics center); integrated services (the physical rehabilitation, MHPSS, surgical, nutritional, food voucher, transport, and case management pathway wrapped around every beneficiary); inclusivity and reintegration (the livelihood support and education reintegration pathway that carries recovered beneficiaries back into economic and social life); and logistics and supply chain (the warehousing, shipment, and procurement capability that keeps prosthetics, components, and assistive devices flowing into Gaza). All four streams operate and are funded, staffed, and managed under this one proposal, with a single Program Manager, a single budget, and a single results framework. There is no financial or operational seam between 'the prosthetics component' and 'the integrated care component': they are one project.
Before describing how these four streams are implemented month by month, it is important to understand the scale of preparatory work RHS has already undertaken to make this program possible. None of the four streams below started from a blank page. Each reflects months of groundwork, institutional coordination, staff recruitment and deployment, market assessment, and infrastructure investment, undertaken by RHS prior to and alongside the submission of this proposal. The subsections that follow describe that preparatory effort for each stream in turn, because the level of effort already invested is itself evidence of RHS's institutional capacity and seriousness of commitment to this program.

### The Service Delivery Network: Fixed Points, Mobile Teams, and the Central Prosthetics Center
The network is designed around a single principle: services must reach beneficiaries where they are, rather than requiring a displaced, mobility-impaired population to reach services. Coverage is structured in three tiers: fixed rehabilitation points for concentrated caseloads, mobile teams for outreach, and one central prosthetics center for specialized fabrication and fitting, so that every beneficiary can access the full care pathway regardless of location, displacement status, or mobility.
Fixed rehabilitation points. RHS will operate fixed rehabilitation points distributed across the Gaza to maximize geographic access. Each point provides physical rehabilitation sessions, MHPSS services (individual and group), nutritional assessment and nutrition education, caregiver care-education sessions, and case management. The points serve as the clinical anchors of the network: beneficiaries identified by the mobile teams are scheduled into them for structured therapy blocks, and each point maintains the treatment spaces, equipment, and confidential counseling spaces required for multidisciplinary care.
Mobile teams. Multidisciplinary mobile teams, each comprising a physiotherapist and an MHPSS counselor, carry the same service package into shelters, camps, temporary learning spaces, and hard-to-reach areas. The mobile teams are the program's identification and continuity engine: they conduct field-level identification and data collection, deliver home visits and pre-fitting preparation, provide rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions to beneficiaries who cannot travel, support caregivers in situ, and maintain follow-up with each case between and after facility-based appointments.
The central prosthetics center (one). One large, fully equipped prosthetics and orthotics center concentrates Gaza's scarce P&O expertise, fabrication equipment, and componentry in a single specialized facility providing casting, fabrication, fitting, alignment, and gait training. Beneficiaries are referred to the center once the technical team confirms pre-fitting readiness, and return to their nearest rehabilitation point or mobile team for continued follow-up after fitting. The center's design, zones, and equipment are described in full in Section 5.5.
The three tiers interlock around the beneficiary rather than around facilities: a case identified by a mobile team in a shelter is registered in KOBO, assessed by the multidisciplinary team, prepared through home visits and sessions at the nearest rehabilitation point, fitted at the central prosthetics center, and followed through gait training back at their point or at home — one record, one case manager, one pathway.

### Preparation: Field Teams and Integrated Services
RHS treats prosthetic fitting and integrated services as a single, indivisible stream of preparatory work, because no patient in this program is fitted with a prosthetic device without simultaneously being enrolled in the rehabilitation, MHPSS, nutrition, transport, and surgical intervention pathway that ensures that the device is actually used. The preparation for this stream is correspondingly built around a single, integrated field team rather than two separate teams assembled independently.
RHS currently fields a team of 13 staff in Gaza dedicated to this stream: five rehabilitation (physiotherapy) staff and five MHPSS staff, in addition to the supporting, logistics, and field management personnel required to coordinate their work. This is not a team RHS proposes to build; it is a team RHS has already recruited, deployed, and is actively managing inside Gaza under extremely difficult operating conditions. The fact that this team is already operational is itself significant preparatory evidence: it means the most operationally difficult part of this program, recruiting, vetting, and deploying qualified clinical staff inside an active conflict zone, has already been accomplished.
This 13-person field team carries responsibility across the full span of the patient pathway, not merely a single point within it. The team identifies beneficiaries through community outreach, MOH referral pathways, and field-level needs assessment; commences pre-fitting activities, including physiotherapy conditioning and psychosocial stabilization, to ensure each patient is clinically and psychologically ready before referral; refers patients to the prosthetics centers for casting and fitting once pre-fitting readiness criteria are met; and continues working with each patient after fitting, because the period immediately following fitting is when the risk of device abandonment is highest and when continued physiotherapy, psychosocial support, and follow-up are most clinically necessary to secure successful long-term device use.
This field team does not operate unsupported. It is backed by an experienced and qualified team based in Amman, which leads clinical quality assurance for the rehabilitation and MHPSS components and supplies the field team with the tools, protocols, and technical knowledge required to deliver this work to a consistently high standard. Because direct physical access into Gaza is a persistent and serious operational constraint, RHS has built a model in which the Amman team provides this support primarily through remote channels, including structured online clinical training and supervision for the Gaza-based rehabilitation and MHPSS staff, so that field staff continuously strengthen their clinical competency even though in-person access is frequently restricted. The Amman team remains in constant contact with the field team specifically to ensure that whatever support is needed — clinical guidance, troubleshooting of difficult cases, technical updates, or simply continuity of communication during periods of access disruption — is available without interruption.

### Preparation: Infrastructure, Equipment, and Supply
The physical infrastructure underpinning the patient service streams required two parallel strands of preparatory work: securing and upgrading suitable facilities, and procuring the specialized equipment and componentry that a P&O workshop requires.
On infrastructure, RHS has rented two locations in Gaza, one situated in the middle of the Gaza Strip and one in the north, selected to maximize geographic access for beneficiaries who, given the severe restrictions on movement within Gaza, would otherwise be unable to reach a single centralized facility. Both locations required substantial work before they could function as rehabilitation and P&O facilities: RHS has invested in major maintenance and rehabilitation of both sites, repairing structural and utility damage and reconfiguring the spaces to the standard required for clinical and fabrication use. These sites anchor the network described above — hosting fixed rehabilitation points and the central prosthetics center — and the remaining rehabilitation point(s) will be commissioned during the mobilization phase to complete the minimum three-point coverage.
On equipment and componentry, RHS has conducted a structured market assessment for P&O equipment and components, surveying suppliers in Jordan and engaging directly with international manufacturers and suppliers to secure the best available pricing without compromising the clinical quality of materials reaching patients. This dual-track sourcing strategy, combining regional procurement through Jordan with direct international supplier relationships, reflects RHS's commitment to ensuring that program funds are utilized as efficiently as possible while maintaining the componentry quality standards required for ISPO-aligned clinical practice. The outcome of this market assessment directly informs the equipment list and budget in Annex 1 and Annex 6.

### Implementation Sequence and Effort
Building on the preparatory groundwork described above, implementation proceeds across three phases. The description below sets out not only what occurs in each phase but the practical effort RHS is undertaking to deliver it, given that a substantial share of this effort is already underway.
Phase 1 covers Months 1 and 2 and is the mobilization phase, in which the preparatory work already described converts into an operational program. On the service delivery network stream, this means commissioning the remaining fixed rehabilitation point(s), completing final installation of equipment at the central prosthetics center, and constituting and training the six mobile teams. On the integrated services stream, it means finalizing the KOBO Toolbox identification and assessment forms, the intake and referral protocols that govern how beneficiaries move from identification through pre-fitting, fitting, and post-fitting follow-up, and the coordination arrangements with the partner hospital for surgical referrals. On the inclusivity stream, it means launching the rapid market assessment that will ground the livelihood component, and confirming with Save the Children International and NRC the temporary learning spaces in which rehabilitation and MHPSS points will be embedded. On the logistics stream, it means positioning the componentry and materials from the June 2026 shipment and confirming the August 2026 shipment pipeline.
Phase 2 covers Months 3 through 12 and is the core delivery phase, in which the identification, assessment, and service delivery workflow operates at full scale: mobile teams identify and register beneficiaries on a rolling basis, the multidisciplinary teams produce tailored service packages, the rehabilitation points and mobile teams deliver physical rehabilitation, MHPSS, nutritional, and food voucher support, and the central prosthetics center scales fitting toward the program's 300-beneficiary target. The effort required in this phase is sustained rather than front-loaded: new beneficiaries present continuously given the ongoing scale of need, and the livelihood and education reintegration pathways begin receiving recovered beneficiaries from the middle of this phase onward. Quarterly joint case reviews across the clinical and inclusivity components ensure that the pace and quality of delivery are checked formally at fixed intervals rather than only at project close.
Phase 3 covers Months 13 through 17 and is the consolidation phase, in which the final cohort of beneficiaries fitted earlier in the program complete their structured post-fitting follow-up and gait training, livelihood projects launched under the inclusivity stream mature with continued RHS follow-up and marketing support from the communication and advocacy team, and children reintegrated into education continue receiving rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions in their learning spaces. This phase is deliberately structured so that the project does not conclude the moment the last device is fitted — the post-fitting follow-up period and the reintegration pathways are treated as core program activity through to project close, not as residual obligations left unaddressed once headline fitting numbers are reached.

### Internal Coordination Across the Four Activity Streams
Because the four activity streams are operationally inseparable for the beneficiary, RHS has designed this as a single, unified project rather than as separately funded components requiring external coordination. Every beneficiary enters the program through a single KOBO-based intake process, run by the unified Gaza field team, that simultaneously triggers clinical screening and integrated care enrollment — there is no pathway by which a beneficiary receives a prosthetic fitting or rehabilitation service without the full pre-service and post-service pathway being initiated around it. Prosthetic fitting records, rehabilitation and MHPSS attendance, nutritional assessments, food voucher disbursements, and livelihood and education referrals are entered into the same clinical database, giving the case manager, the P&O specialist, and the rehabilitation, MHPSS, nutrition, and inclusivity teams a single unified beneficiary record rather than fragmented files. The multidisciplinary team — P&O specialist, physiotherapist, MHPSS counselor, nutritionist, and case manager — meets at a minimum of every four weeks per beneficiary cohort to review progress and agree coordinated remediation for any beneficiary at risk of disengaging from any part of the pathway. All four activity streams report into the same Program Manager position and the same Program Oversight Committee, and are resourced from the same project budget.

## Detailed Implementation Pathway: From Identification to Reintegration
This section sets out, step by step, how a beneficiary moves through the program — from the first knock on a shelter door to the closure of their case file — and who is responsible for quality at each step. The pathway is specified deliberately at this level of detail because, in RHS's operational experience, it is the discipline of the workflow, not merely the availability of any single service, that determines whether an integrated program delivers integrated outcomes.

### Beneficiary Identification and Data Collection (KOBO Toolbox)
Identification begins in the field. The six mobile teams — supported by community outreach volunteers, Ministry of Health referral channels, Health Cluster partners, and RHS's presence at the fixed rehabilitation points — actively identify persons with disabilities, including amputees and TBI and SCI survivors, in shelters, camps, host communities, and hard-to-reach areas. Self-referral and family referral are equally supported through the rehabilitation points and RHS's community networks.
Every identified case is registered through a standardized digital identification form built on the KOBO Toolbox platform and administered by trained data collectors on tablets in the field. The identification form is comprehensive: it captures the beneficiary's demographic and contact information; displacement status and current location; injury and amputation profile (level, side, cause, and date); TBI/SCI clinical presentation where applicable; prior services received; current functional and mobility status; psychological screening indicators; nutritional status; household composition and caregiver situation; food security status; school enrollment status for children; and the household's economic situation and pre-injury livelihood. Because the form covers everything about the beneficiary and their family — not the injury alone — it provides the complete evidence base from which a tailored service package is developed for each case.
The data workflow is structured and auditable. Completed forms are submitted from the field to the central KOBO server in real time, or cached offline and synchronized when connectivity allows — a routine necessity in Gaza. RHS officers then follow up on the quality of the collected data: incoming submissions are reviewed daily for completeness, consistency, and duplicate detection, and substandard forms are returned to the collecting team for field correction before the case proceeds.

### Data Review, Analysis, and Individual Service Planning
Once the field officers have verified data quality, the M&E unit and the technical unit review and analyze the dataset. The M&E unit runs completeness and consistency audits, monitors caseload composition against program targets (gender, age, amputation level, geography), and produces the analytical outputs that inform program steering. The technical unit — the program's senior clinical staff across P&O, physiotherapy, MHPSS, and nutrition — reviews each case record clinically and shares the plan for each individual: a costed, scheduled, individually tailored service package translated directly from the identification form's evidence.

### The Tailored Service Package
Every enrolled beneficiary receives a written, individualized service package developed from their identification record, specifying: the number of physical rehabilitation sessions required and their delivery point (fixed rehabilitation point, mobile team, or home visit); the number of MHPSS sessions required, for the beneficiary and — where assessed as needed — for their caregivers; nutritional support requirements, including whether the household needs food vouchers and for how many months; whether surgical intervention is required before rehabilitation or fitting can proceed, together with the referral arrangements to the partner hospital; the assistive devices required, distributed on the basis of assessed need; and, for amputees, the pre-fitting preparation program and the projected referral window to the prosthetics center.
The package is reviewed with the beneficiary and their family, formally consented, and entered into the case management system, where it becomes the reference against which every subsequent session, visit, and referral is tracked. Packages are living documents: they are updated at each multidisciplinary case review as the beneficiary progresses.

### Home Visits and Pre-Fitting Services
With the service package agreed, the team begins home visits and case-level follow-up. For amputees, the pre-fitting phase is the crucial determinant of continuity and long-term success: the physiotherapy team delivers stump conditioning, desensitization, strengthening, and contracture prevention; the nutrition team works to stabilize nutritional status so that limb volume is stable enough for accurate casting and durable socket fit; and the MHPSS team prepares the beneficiary psychologically for fitting and for the rehabilitation effort it demands. RHS treats pre-fitting readiness as a formal clinical gate: no beneficiary is referred for casting until the technical team confirms readiness, because fitting a device to an unprepared residual limb predictably produces pain, poor fit, and abandonment.
For TBI and SCI beneficiaries, the same home-visit structure delivers positioning and mobility training, caregiver-assisted exercise programs, pressure-injury prevention, continence management education where relevant, and assistive device training — all calibrated to the individual plan.

### Caregiver Support: MHPSS and Care-Education Sessions
During the home-visit and pre-fitting phase, the program deliberately works with the family as well as the beneficiary. MHPSS sessions are provided to caregivers where the assessment identifies a need — recognizing that caregiver exhaustion, grief, and distress are among the most common causes of beneficiary disengagement. In parallel, the physiotherapy team delivers structured physical rehabilitation care-education sessions for caregivers, training them in the best practices for supporting the beneficiary: safe transfers, home exercise supervision, stump bandaging and hygiene, skin checks, positioning, and the early warning signs that require the team's attention. A supported and skilled caregiver multiplies the effect of every professional session delivered.

### Referral to the Prosthetics Center and Fitting
When the technical team confirms the readiness of the case, the beneficiary is referred to the nearest P&O center to complete the fitting. At the center, the P&O team completes clinical assessment, casting, socket fabrication, static and dynamic alignment, and initial gait training, following the technical specifications in the individual plan. Transport and accompaniment are arranged for beneficiaries who cannot travel independently, with female accompaniment for women and girls and family accompaniment for children.

### Post-Fitting Follow-Up, Gait Training, and Recovery
Fitting is the midpoint of the journey, not its end. After fitting, the team continues the follow-up and gait training — at the rehabilitation points, through the mobile teams, and at home — until the beneficiary shows full recovery against the functional goals in their individual plan: confident, safe ambulation on the device; independence in donning, doffing, and daily device care; a stable, well-tolerated socket fit; and documented mobility outcomes on the program's standard measures. Follow-up appointments monitor residual limb health, socket fit as limb volume changes, and device condition, with adjustments completed at the center as needed.

### Discharge and Referral to the Inclusivity Team
A beneficiary who reaches full recovery is not discharged into a vacuum. At recovery, the case is formally reviewed and, where the beneficiary is within the criteria, referred onward to the inclusivity team: adults meeting the livelihood criteria enter the livelihood support pathway described in Section 5.4, and children are supported back into education — the RHS team coordinates with the nearest educational point, registers the child in it, and continues the child's rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions within the school setting. This warm-handover design ensures that clinical recovery converts into economic and social reintegration, which is the program's ultimate measure of success.

## Inclusivity: Livelihood Support and Education Reintegration
The inclusivity team owns the program's reintegration mandate: livelihood support for adults and education reintegration for children. Both pathways receive beneficiaries referred by the clinical teams upon recovery, and both are designed so that the gains achieved through rehabilitation convert into durable economic and social participation rather than ending at clinical discharge.

### Livelihood Support for 20% of Beneficiaries
Twenty percent of program beneficiaries will be supported with livelihood activities, prioritizing those who are within the program's criteria: completed rehabilitation goals, working age, household economic vulnerability, and a viable project concept or prior trade. Support packages combine business development guidance, in-kind start-up assets or grants, and adaptive equipment where the beneficiary's disability requires workplace adaptation.
The livelihood component is grounded in evidence, not assumption: it will be implemented only after a rapid market assessment, conducted at program mobilization, which maps viable market niches, demand, supply chains, and price points across the operating areas. Each supported project is selected and shaped against the assessment's findings to ensure the sustainability of the projects beneficiaries will be implementing — avoiding market saturation and matching beneficiaries' skills and physical capacities to genuinely viable opportunities.
Support does not end at project launch. The RHS team will continue following up with each livelihood beneficiary — monitoring project health, troubleshooting difficulties, and connecting beneficiaries to further opportunities — while RHS's communication and advocacy team supports beneficiaries with the marketing plans for their projects, including product presentation, local market linkages, and visibility through RHS's community networks and platforms.

### Education Reintegration for Children
For children, reintegration means school. Reintegrating children into education is the inclusivity team's second core task, pursued case by case: for every child beneficiary, the RHS team coordinates with the nearest educational point, registers the child in it, and then continues the child's rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions inside the school setting, so that returning to education never means interrupting clinical care.
RHS is working with Save the Children International and the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) to establish specialized rehabilitation and MHPSS points within the temporary learning spaces. Embedding services in learning spaces is deliberately better for the children across multiple dimensions: it surrounds them with peer support, normalizes their return to childhood routines, strengthens their mental status through structured daily activity, and combines reintegration in education activities with continuing therapy in a single, child-friendly location.
RHS also provides MHPSS training to the teachers in the educational points that have children with amputation enrolled, equipping them to cover follow-up with all children, recognize distress, practice the best approach in supporting children with disabilities, and sustain an inclusive classroom environment well beyond the program period.

## The Central Prosthetics Center

### Strategic Importance
The central prosthetics center is the physical backbone of the prosthetic component of this program. Without a properly equipped, safety-compliant, professionally organized fabrication and fitting facility, prosthetic service delivery cannot proceed to international standards. The center serves four functions simultaneously: it is the clinical service site for the casting, fabrication, fitting, and gait training of the program's funded prosthetic beneficiaries; it is the fabrication hub in which the componentry and raw materials from RHS's supply pipeline are converted into finished, individually fitted devices; it is the referral destination for every case confirmed ready by the field teams across the rehabilitation points and mobile teams; and it is a demonstration facility that establishes the physical standard for P&O service delivery in Gaza. RHS's approach to the center's design follows ISPO recommended facility standards [19].

Zone 10, the Rehabilitation Department, physically embeds the integrated care model within the center itself. Every patient who arrives for prosthetic fitting can be immediately assessed by the physiotherapy, MHPSS, and nutrition teams in the same facility, without the access, transport, and coordination barriers that fragment care in typical humanitarian settings.

### Why Zone 10 Is Co-Located Rather Than Referred Out
RHS deliberately designed the center to include Zone 10 as an integral architectural component rather than relying on referral to a separate physiotherapy clinic, a separate MHPSS center, or a separate nutrition point elsewhere in Gaza. This design decision was not incidental, it directly addresses one of the most consistently documented causes of integrated care pathway failure in fragmented humanitarian service systems: patients who are referred from a prosthetics fitting site to a separate facility for physiotherapy, MHPSS, or nutritional support frequently do not complete the referral, because of transport barriers, security and access constraints, the burden of repeated travel for patients with limited mobility, and the practical difficulty of coordinating appointments across multiple unconnected facilities and providers [4, 15].
By co-locating the integrated care functions within the same facility where prosthetic casting, fitting, and follow-up occur, RHS removes the single largest structural barrier to integrated care pathway completion. A patient attending a scheduled prosthetic follow-up appointment can, in the same visit and without additional travel, be seen by the physiotherapist for gait progression, by the MHPSS counsellor for a scheduled psychosocial support session, and by the nutrition team for a follow-up nutritional assessment. This is not a convenience feature, it is a primary determinant of whether the >85% device retention rate achieved by genuinely integrated programs is realistic for this project, as opposed to the 15-30% retention rate typical of programs that nominally offer integrated services but deliver them through uncoordinated, geographically dispersed referral [22].
Zone 10's staffing, physiotherapist, MHPSS counsellor, nutritionist, and case manager, is funded and managed under this same project, as part of the unified integrated services stream; the space is built, equipped, and maintained as part of the center's infrastructure described in this section, and the staff who work within it report into the same Program Manager and budget line as the prosthetics service team.

## Holistic Patient Care and Integrated Service Delivery

### The Evidence for Integration: Why Prosthetics Alone Is Never Enough
The humanitarian rehabilitation literature contains a clear and consistent finding: prosthetic device provision in the absence of concurrent rehabilitation, psychosocial support, and nutritional care produces outcomes that are clinically, functionally, and economically indistinguishable from providing no intervention at all. Abandonment rates of 70 to 90% in device-only programs have been documented across multiple conflict settings, including Cambodia, South Sudan, Afghanistan, and Syria [15, 17, 22]. In Gaza specifically, RHS's operational data documents an abandonment rate exceeding 80% in fragmented programs that do not provide integrated follow-up care [4].
The mechanisms of this failure are well understood and documented in the clinical literature. Prosthetic devices in conflict settings are fitted to individuals who are simultaneously experiencing: residual limb volume fluctuations due to malnutrition and dehydration, which cause socket fit to deteriorate within days of fitting, producing pain and skin breakdown [14]; post-traumatic psychological responses including hypervigilance, pain catastrophizing, and avoidance behaviors that prevent engagement with gait training and device wear [16]; absence of physiotherapy support to guide progressive loading, strengthen residual limb musculature, and correct gait deviations that would otherwise produce secondary injury; and logistical barriers, transport, security, cost, that prevent return to clinic for the follow-up adjustments that every new prosthetic fitting requires.
The review on prosthetic outcomes in humanitarian settings demonstrates that the single strongest predictor of successful long-term device retention is not device quality, not fitting technique, and not component selection; it is the presence of an integrated, multidisciplinary rehabilitation team supporting the patient through the full care continuum from fitting through rehabilitation to community reintegration [15]. Darnall et al. further demonstrate that unaddressed psychological distress is an independent predictor of prosthetic abandonment, with PTSD, depression, and catastrophizing specifically linked to non-use devices even when devices are technically well-fitted [16]. The ICRC's Physical Rehabilitation Programme global data, collected across 33 countries, consistently shows that integrated programs achieve device retention rates exceeding 85% at 12 months, compared to 15-30% in device-only programs [22].
Nutritional status has a direct and well-documented effect on wound healing, skin integrity, and the physical tolerance of prosthetic loading. In Gaza, where 90% of children under two are in extreme food poverty and acute malnutrition is widespread across all age groups [14], fitting a prosthetic device without concurrent nutritional support to a malnourished individual produces predictable clinical failure: the socket rapidly loses fit as limb volume decreases, skin breakdown occurs over bony prominences, wound infection is poorly resisted by a nutritionally compromised immune system, and the patient must discontinue wear before any therapeutic benefit is achieved. Addressing nutritional status before and during prosthetic fitting is not ancillary care — it is a clinical prerequisite for device retention and rehabilitation success.

### The RHS Integrated Care Model: Structure and Principles
RHS's integrated care model is built on the principle that every prosthetic beneficiary must receive simultaneous access to physical rehabilitation, mental health and psychosocial support, and nutritional care as a non-negotiable package. This principle is embedded in RHS's organizational mandate: RHS does not fund or implement prosthetic services without a funded, operational integrated care pathway for the same beneficiaries. This is not a programmatic preference, it is an organizational policy derived directly from the evidence base described above and from RHS's own operational experience in Gaza.
For this program, all beneficiaries will simultaneously receive the following services, in the dosages specified in their individual tailored service packages, funded and delivered as a core, integrated component of this single project:
Care Domain
Service Content
Provider / Platform
Prosthetic Fitting and Follow-Up
Initial assessment; casting; fabrication; fitting; alignment; gait training introduction; device adjustment; minimum 3 scheduled follow-up appointments; emergency adjustment as needed
RHS P&O team at the central prosthetics center
Physical Rehabilitation
Pre-fitting stump conditioning; progressive post-fitting loading protocol; structured gait training and progression; strength and balance rehabilitation; community reintegration functional training; home exercise program with caregiver training
RHS physiotherapy team
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS)
Individual psychological assessment ; group psychosocial support sessions (minimum 6); individual counseling for patients presenting with clinical-level distress; PTSD screening and specialist referral; family inclusion sessions
RHS MHPSS team
Nutritional Support and Assessment
Nutritional status assessment at intake and at each follow-up; referral to therapeutic feeding programs for malnutrition cases; high-protein dietary supplementation during the acute post-fitting phase; nutritional education for patients and caregivers; food vouchers for food-insecure households, for the number of months specified in the individual care plan
RHS Nutrition team
Transport and Accompaniment

Surgical intervention
