### Patient Referral and Intake Pathway
Patient referral follows a structured five-step pathway designed to ensure that only clinically appropriate candidates enter the program, that all patients are consented and enrolled in the integrated care package from the first point of contact, and that the patient case mix reflects the priority subgroups (women, children, bilateral amputees, high-level cases).
• Referral: Patients are referred by Gaza Ministry of Health rehabilitation coordinators, ICRC, MSF, WHO-supported facilities, and community health workers affiliated with RHS's Gaza network.
• Screening: All referred patients undergo a clinical screening assessment by RHS team.
• Multi-disciplinary assessment: Patients who pass clinical screening undergo simultaneous assessment by the P&O Specialist (clinical/prosthetic), the physiotherapy team (rehabilitation readiness), the MHPSS team (psychological status and support needs), and the nutrition team (nutritional status and wound healing capacity).
• Enrollment and consent: Patients meeting clinical criteria are enrolled in the program with full informed consent covering the prosthetic fitting process, the integrated care package, the use of anonymized data for monitoring and reporting, and the right to withdraw without consequence, for those who does not meet clinical criteria they will be referred to the partner hospital for surgical intervention with close follow up by RHS team to continue with them once they are fully healed and ready for the pre-fitting services
• Case assignment and care plan: A case manager is assigned, an individualized care plan produced, and the patient's care pathway formally initiated across all domains simultaneously.

### Pediatric and Gender-Sensitive Provisions
Children constitute a significant proportion of Gaza's new amputation caseload; Gaza Ministry of Health documents 15 children per day acquiring a lifelong disability during the conflict [11, 12]. Pediatric prosthetic cases present specific clinical challenges: rapidly changing limb volume with growth, the need for growth-responsive socket systems, the importance of school reintegration, and the requirement for family-centered care planning addressing caregiver stress and capacity. RHS's program addresses these needs through: pediatric-specific clinical protocols; a dedicated pediatric psychological support stream within the MHPSS component; school liaison support for school-aged children; and caregiver training in socket management and follow-up care.
Female amputees face particular barriers in Gaza's social context: cultural norms around examination by male practitioners, the potential absence of female family accompaniment, and the psychological impact of disfigurement and disability within specific gender role frameworks. RHS addresses these barriers through: the deployment of female practitioners across the rehabilitation points, mobile teams, and the center; the provision of female patient accompaniment services; the availability of female MHPSS counselors; and gender-sensitive consultation scheduling and facility design.

### Service Frequency and Dosage Standards
To ensure that the integrated care pathway is not merely a list of available services but a defined, auditable schedule of care, RHS specifies minimum frequency and dosage standards for each component of the pathway. These standards form the basis of the adherence indicators tracked in the evaluation framework and are reviewed at every quarterly case review.
Service
Minimum Frequency / Dosage
Clinical Rationale
Physiotherapy
Pre-fitting conditioning: 2x/week for a minimum of 2 weeks, where clinically indicated. Post-fitting: weekly for first 6 weeks, then biweekly through Month 6, minimum 4 documented sessions overall
Progressive loading and gait training are the primary clinical mechanisms preventing falls, gait compensation injuries, and secondary musculoskeletal complications [15]
MHPSS
Individual psychological assessment; minimum 6 group psychosocial sessions across the first 3 months; individual counseling on a needs basis for patients meeting clinical distress thresholds
PTSD, depression, and catastrophizing are independent predictors of device abandonment, even with technically excellent fitting [16]
Nutrition
Nutritional assessment at identification, at fitting, and at each scheduled follow-up (minimum 4 assessments over 6 months); therapeutic feeding referral within 1 week for any patient meeting acute malnutrition thresholds
Malnourished patients lose socket fit as limb volume changes and are at materially higher risk of skin breakdown and wound infection [14]
Transport and Accompaniment
Provided for every scheduled appointment for patients assessed as unable to self-mobilize safely, and for all female patients and pediatric cases requiring accompaniment
Removing the single largest documented barrier to integrated care pathway completion in fragmented service systems [4]
Case Management
Single named case manager assigned at identification; MDT case conference minimum every 6 weeks per patient cohort; case closure summary at 6-month follow-up
Continuity of a single accountable point of contact is associated with materially higher pathway completion rates in humanitarian rehabilitation programming [17]
These dosage standards are minimums, not targets. Individual care plans produced at identification may specify a higher frequency of any service based on clinical need, for example, a child with a bilateral amputation and documented acute malnutrition would receive physiotherapy, MHPSS, and nutrition support well above these floors.

### Illustrative Patient Journey
To make the integrated care pathway concrete rather than abstract, RHS sets out below a composite, anonymized illustrative case representative of the patient profile this program is designed to serve. This is not an individual patient's data; it is a composite drawn from RHS's Gaza operational experience, constructed to illustrate how the components described throughout this proposal function together across a single patient's care.
A 9-year-old girl is identified by a mobile team with a transtibial amputation sustained eight months earlier, her family having been displaced twice since the injury. At identification through the KOBO-based assessment, the multidisciplinary team identifies acute malnutrition, limiting safe socket fitting until nutritional status stabilizes; pronounced anxiety symptoms consistent with conflict-related trauma; and a residual limb requiring pre-fitting conditioning before casting. Over the following weeks, the nutrition team enrolls her in therapeutic feeding and provides a food voucher for her family, while the MHPSS counsellor begins age-appropriate psychosocial support sessions with family inclusion, and the physiotherapist begins pre-fitting strengthening through home visits. Once nutritional and psychological readiness criteria are met — typically four to six weeks — casting, fabrication, and fitting proceed at the central prosthetics center. Following fitting, she receives weekly physiotherapy for gait training, continued MHPSS support, and nutritional follow-up at each appointment; the inclusivity team registers her at the nearest educational point, where her rehabilitation and MHPSS sessions continue within the temporary learning space supported by RHS's collaboration with Save the Children International and NRC, and her teachers receive MHPSS training. Transport is arranged for each visit given her family's displacement and lack of reliable transport access. At six-month follow-up, she is recorded in the clinical database as retaining and using her device, attending school, and reporting improved mobility on the PLUS-M tool — an outcome that would be statistically unlikely had any single component of this pathway been absent.

### Why This Project Funds the Full Pathway Rather Than Prosthetics Alone
RHS has deliberately structured this as a single, unified project that funds the service delivery network, prosthetic service delivery, and the full integrated care, livelihood, and education reintegration pathway together, rather than presenting prosthetics as a standalone intervention and treating rehabilitation, MHPSS, nutrition, and food security as a donor's optional add-on or a separately funded companion initiative. This is a programmatic decision, not an administrative default. A donor funding a prosthetics-only project, however well-intentioned, would in practice be funding an intervention that the evidence base shows fails for the majority of patients: device abandonment in isolated prosthetic programs exceeds 80% [15]. By contrast, the integrated model — funded, staffed, and managed as one program under this proposal — is what makes the prosthetic investment effective: every dollar spent on fabrication and fitting is paired with the rehabilitation, psychological, nutritional, and reintegration support required for that device to remain on the patient's limb and deliver lasting functional benefit. RHS's own field data from Gaza confirms this is not a theoretical risk but an operational reality [4].

## Assistive Devices: Need-Based Distribution and Community Circulation
Beyond prosthetics, the program distributes assistive devices — wheelchairs, crutches, walkers, and other mobility and self-care aids — strictly on the basis of assessed need. The need for assistive devices is captured as part of the evaluation of each case: the multidisciplinary assessment and the tailored service package specify which devices are required, and every distribution is recorded in the beneficiary's file, with training provided on safe use and maintenance.
One of the success stories that RHS is proud to highlight is the community circulation of assistive devices: beneficiaries who improve and no longer need their devices donate them to another case. This practice, which emerged organically among RHS's beneficiaries, reduces cost, increases community cohesion, and ensures the best utilization of the budget — each donated device is inspected, refurbished where needed, and re-issued through the same need-based assessment process, so that a single procured device can serve more than one recovery journey.

## Logistics, Supply Chain, and Procurement

### Warehousing and the Shipment Pipeline
Logistics is the biggest challenge for any project implementation in Gaza, and RHS has built its operating model around that reality. RHS maintains warehouses in both Gaza and Amman, giving it the capacity to pre-position, store, and stage materials on both sides of the access pipeline. To move goods into Gaza, RHS works through an established set of relationships with WHO, WFP, international NGOs, and the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization (JHCO) in Jordan, all of which support the shipment of humanitarian cargo into the Strip.
This pipeline is proven, not theoretical. On 15 June 2026, RHS successfully delivered a shipment of approximately 800 prosthetics into Gaza — one of the largest prosthetic consignments to enter the Strip during the current crisis. In the same shipment, RHS moved components and equipment on behalf of two other partner organizations working in prosthetics in Gaza, reflecting RHS's role as a supply-chain enabler for the wider sector rather than for its own program alone. A further prosthetics shipment is planned for August 2026, and in the next shipments RHS is planning to bring in prosthetics and raw materials for all the actors in the sector, to ensure continuity of services across all the workshops and locations delivering P&O care in Gaza.

### Evidence-Based Procurement: The RHS Needs Formula
For the procurement of prosthetics and assistive devices, RHS procures to need rather than to guesswork. Drawing on its operational experience, RHS has developed a procurement formula built on previous and ongoing data collection and its continuously updated beneficiary database. The formula specifies the percentage distribution of the caseload by children, female, and male beneficiaries; by upper-limb versus lower-limb amputation; and by below-joint versus above-joint amputation level — all of which are taken into consideration in sizing and specifying each order. The formula is recalibrated as new identification data flows in through the KOBO system, so that each shipment's composition mirrors the actual clinical profile of the caseload awaiting fitting.
RHS is also technology agnostic: it is not tied to any single manufacturer, componentry system, or fabrication technology. This allows RHS to procure based on the needs of each beneficiary profile, and in a way that guarantees clinical appropriateness, availability, price competitiveness, and continuity of supply — selecting, for each case and each order, the technology that best serves the beneficiary rather than a predetermined brand commitment.

title: Evaluation Plan
content:
## MEAL Philosophy
RHS's MEAL system for this program is designed to simultaneously serve multiple purposes: real-time program management (enabling course corrections before problems compound); donor accountability (providing verified, documented evidence of performance against indicators); learning and knowledge generation (producing findings that inform the design of future integrated rehabilitation programs across the region); and beneficiary accountability (ensuring that beneficiaries and their families have structured and safe mechanisms to raise concerns and influence program delivery). Consistent with the integrated program design described throughout this proposal, RHS's MEAL system does not monitor prosthetic and rehabilitation service outcomes in isolation from integrated care pathway adherence — the two are tracked in the same clinical database, reported in the same indicator set, and reviewed by the same Program Oversight Committee at the same quarterly sessions, so that a deterioration in integrated care adherence is visible to program management at the same time, and with the same priority, as a deterioration in fitting or rehabilitation quality.

## Field Data Quality Monitoring
Because every service decision in this program flows from field-collected data, data quality is monitored as rigorously as clinical quality. The KOBO Toolbox data collection workflow described in Section 5.3 is supervised through a layered quality assurance structure: field officers review all incoming submissions daily for completeness, consistency, and duplication, returning substandard forms for field correction; supervisors re-verify a sample of submitted forms against beneficiaries in person through weekly spot-checks; and the M&E unit conducts monthly data audits across the full dataset before analysis is released to the technical unit for service planning. All data collection complies with RHS's data protection protocols, with informed consent recorded at registration and access restricted by role.

## Patient Outcome Monitoring
Patient outcomes are monitored through a structured data collection system administered by the case management team, with data entered into a secure digital database maintained under RHS's data protection protocols. All patient outcome data is anonymized for reporting. Key monitoring points are: intake (clinical assessment data, baseline mobility and quality-of-life scores), fitting (technical fitting data, initial satisfaction), 6-week follow-up, 3-month follow-up, and 6-month follow-up. Integrated care pathway adherence — attendance at physiotherapy, MHPSS, and nutrition appointments — is tracked in the same system to ensure that the holistic care model is operationally functional for every patient, not merely nominally provided.
Primary outcome measures are: the Prosthetic Limb Users Survey of Mobility (PLUS-M) for mobility outcomes [21]; the SIGAM Mobility Grade for clinical mobility classification; and device retention rate at 6 months. Secondary measures include: pain scores (numeric rating scale); quality of life (adapted EQ-5D); and integrated care pathway completion rate (defined as attending minimum 2 MHPSS sessions, 1 nutritional assessment, and 4 physiotherapy sessions during the program period).

## RHS Digital Innovation: In-House Developed Monitoring Platform
A central element of RHS's monitoring and evaluation capability is a digital platform developed in-house by RHS specifically for its rehabilitation programs. Rather than relying on fragmented spreadsheets or generic third-party tools, RHS has invested in building a single, secure, purpose-built system that captures the full beneficiary record — from KOBO-based identification and multidisciplinary assessment through fitting, integrated care attendance, and six-month follow-up — in a single unified database. The platform allows the case management team, the P&O specialists, and the physiotherapy, MHPSS, and nutrition teams to work from the same real-time record, so that integrated care pathway adherence is visible alongside clinical outcomes rather than tracked in isolation.
For this program, the platform generates real-time dashboards against each of the key performance indicators , enabling program management to identify and correct emerging problems before they compound, and giving the Program Oversight Committee and the donor verified, up-to-date evidence of performance. All patient data held in the platform is anonymized for reporting and maintained under RHS's data protection protocols. The detailed results-based logical framework, linking inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and goal-level indicators with their means of verification and assumptions, is being developed as a separate document (Annex 2) and will operate within this same platform.

## Evaluation and Reporting
A mid-term internal evaluation will be conducted at Month 9, assessing progress against all indicators, service delivery performance across the rehabilitation points, mobile teams, and the central prosthetics center, patient outcome data, and any programmatic challenges requiring structural response. A final independent evaluation will be conducted at Month 17 by an external evaluator with experience in the P&O sector, producing a comprehensive report covering effectiveness, efficiency, coherence, sustainability, and lessons learned.
Donor reporting follows the schedule agreed in the grant agreement, with at least quarterly narrative and financial reports. All patient data in reports is anonymized. Case studies and photographic documentation are produced with full informed consent and in compliance with the RHS's child safeguarding and protection policies.

title: Partnerships and Coordination
content:
No single organization can respond to disability needs at Gaza's current scale. RHS has therefore built this program on a deliberate architecture of partnerships — normative, operational, and logistical — that multiplies its reach, prevents duplication, and anchors the program within the coordinated humanitarian response.

## WHO and the Health Cluster
RHS works with the World Health Organization and the Health Cluster to ensure a coordinated response across Gaza's rehabilitation sector. RHS participates in Health Cluster coordination mechanisms and reporting, aligning its geographic footprint and caseload with cluster-wide service mapping so that the fixed rehabilitation points, the mobile team routes, and the central prosthetics center complement rather than duplicate the services of other actors. RHS contributes its beneficiary and needs data — appropriately anonymized — to the cluster's collective needs analysis, and coordinates its referral pathways with cluster partners so that a beneficiary identified by any actor in the system can reach the service they require. WHO is also a critical partner on access and supply, having supported the movement of RHS's prosthetic shipments into Gaza.

## Rehabilitation, P&O, and MHPSS Partners
RHS works closely with all the partners delivering rehabilitation, prosthetics and orthotics, and MHPSS services in Gaza, to ensure that the sector operates as a single continuum of care rather than a set of parallel programs. This cooperation takes concrete, operational forms: harmonized clinical and data standards so that cases can move between actors without loss of information; mutual case referrals, so that beneficiaries are served by whichever actor is nearest and best placed; joint technical exchange on complex cases; and — most distinctively — RHS's role as a supply-chain enabler for the whole sector. The June 2026 shipment carried components and equipment on behalf of two partner organizations working in prosthetics in Gaza, and the forthcoming shipments are planned to bring in prosthetics and raw materials for all the actors, ensuring continuity of services across all the workshops and locations delivering P&O care in Gaza.

## Education Partners: Save the Children International and NRC
For education reintegration, RHS partners with Save the Children International and the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), embedding specialized rehabilitation and MHPSS points within the temporary learning spaces they operate. The partnership pairs RHS's clinical capabilities with the partners' education infrastructure and child-protection expertise, giving child beneficiaries peer support, daily routine, and continuing therapy in a single child-friendly setting, and extends to the MHPSS training RHS provides to teachers in the educational points attended by children with amputation.

## Logistics Partners: WHO, WFP, JHCO, and International NGOs
RHS's supply pipeline into Gaza runs through an established set of logistics partnerships: WHO and the World Food Programme (WFP) on humanitarian cargo movement and access facilitation, the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organization (JHCO) as the principal Jordanian shipment channel, and a network of international NGOs supporting consolidation and clearance. These relationships — proven by the delivery of approximately 800 prosthetics on 15 June 2026 — are managed from RHS's Amman logistics base and warehouse network, and are described in full in the Logistics, Supply Chain, and Procurement section of this proposal.

## Ministry of Health and the Surgical Partner Hospital
RHS operates within the Ministry of Health framework: MOH referral channels are one of the program's primary identification pathways, the program's data standards are aligned with MOH systems, and the program design is consistent with the Palestinian National Rehabilitation Strategy 2024–2028 [23]. For surgical intervention, RHS maintains a formal referral arrangement with a partner hospital, through which beneficiaries whose tailored service package identifies surgical need receive surgical care with a coordinated handback into the rehabilitation pathway once they are ready to proceed.

title: Impact – Sustainability, Scale-up
content:
This program has been designed so that its impact outlives its funding period. Sustainability is engineered into the program's architecture at five levels — institutional, sectoral, community, economic, and strategic — each described below.

## Local Ownership and Continuity of Services
The program is delivered by Gaza-based teams from day one: the staff of the rehabilitation points, the six mobile teams, and the central prosthetics center are drawn from Gaza's own health workforce, clinically supervised and continuously strengthened through the structured remote supervision provided by the Amman hub — so that every month of program delivery deepens the clinical competency that remains in Gaza after project close. The physical infrastructure the program leaves behind is equally durable: the two rehabilitated facilities, the fully equipped central prosthetics center, and the fixed rehabilitation points remain functional beyond the funding period, as does the KOBO-based beneficiary database and case management system, which constitutes a lasting information asset for Gaza's rehabilitation sector. Because the program operates within the Ministry of Health framework and its referral pathways, its services are institutionally anchored rather than parallel.

## Sector-Wide Supply Continuity
RHS's logistics model deliberately sustains the whole sector, not only this program. The June 2026 shipment carried components and equipment for two partner organizations working in prosthetics in Gaza, and the follow-on shipments — beginning August 2026 — are being designed to bring in prosthetics and raw materials for all the actors in the sector, keeping every workshop and P&O location in Gaza operational. Combined with RHS's technology-agnostic procurement policy and the continuously recalibrated needs formula, this ensures that the flow of components and materials mirrors the sector's real caseload and does not collapse when any single program ends.

## Community-Level Sustainability
Every caregiver care-education session transfers clinical skills into a household, where they remain: safe transfers, stump care, home exercise supervision, and early-warning recognition continue protecting the beneficiary long after the formal sessions end. The MHPSS training delivered to teachers in the educational points equips the learning spaces themselves to sustain follow-up and inclusive practice for all children. And the community circulation of assistive devices — beneficiaries donating devices they no longer need for inspection, refurbishment, and reissue — is a beneficiary-led sustainability mechanism that reduces cost, strengthens community cohesion, and maximizes the utilization of every device procured.

## Economic Sustainability of Livelihood Projects
The livelihood component is built for durability rather than disbursement: projects are selected only after the rapid market assessment confirms genuinely viable demand, the RHS team continues following up on each project's health after launch, and the communication and advocacy team supports every beneficiary's marketing plan. The result is a portfolio of income-generating projects designed to survive in Gaza's real market conditions, converting a one-time program investment into continuing household income for 20% of the program's beneficiaries.

## Scale-Up Pathway
The program's model is deliberately replicable and expandable. The service network scales horizontally — additional rehabilitation points and mobile teams can be added without redesign; the KOBO identification workflow, the procurement needs formula, and the monitoring platform scale with caseload at marginal cost; and the Amman–Gaza logistics pipeline has already demonstrated that it can move sector-scale volumes. RHS's 2026–2028 Strategic Plan positions this program as the operational foundation for expanded rehabilitation coverage across Gaza, in alignment with WHO's Rehabilitation 2030 framework and the Palestinian National Rehabilitation Strategy 2024–2028 [5, 23].

## Communication, Visibility, and Media Strategy
RHS's communication strategy for this project serves three mutually reinforcing objectives: demonstrating impact to the donor and accountability to the public; advocating for sustained international investment in Gaza's rehabilitation workforce and in integrated rehabilitation programming; and amplifying the voices and stories of beneficiaries in ways that restore their dignity and agency rather than reducing them to victims.
Storytelling and Human-Centered Documentation
The program's most powerful communication assets are the individual stories of beneficiaries whose lives are transformed by high-quality prosthetic and rehabilitation care embedded in a full holistic care pathway. RHS will systematically capture: patient narratives — produced with full informed consent and clinical sensitivity — illustrating restoration of independence, mobility, and social participation; beneficiary success stories from the livelihood and education reintegration pathways, including the community circulation of assistive devices; and documented outcomes showing measurable improvements in mobility scores, device retention, and quality of life at follow-up.
RHS's communication products will consistently reflect the integrated nature of the care model rather than presenting prosthetic fitting as a standalone clinical event. A patient story produced for donor or public communication will, where consented and clinically appropriate, reference the physiotherapy, MHPSS, or nutritional support that accompanied the prosthetic fitting, so that the public understands the full scope of what restoring a patient's mobility actually requires, rather than reducing the achievement to the device alone. This is both an accuracy commitment and an advocacy choice: it is the most direct way RHS can use this program's communications to build donor and public understanding of why integrated rehabilitation funding matters, not only for this program but across the wider humanitarian sector.
Media Engagement and Public Advocacy
• Program Launch Event: A formal launch for local health authorities, MOH representatives, partner organizations, and media.
• Monthly Community Forums: Community-facing sessions on rehabilitation services, disability inclusion, and prosthetics accessibility.
• Quarterly Media Releases: Written releases sharing program milestones and data highlights, distributed to national and international media.
• Partnership Announcements: Formal communications marking key partnership milestones with WHO, the Health Cluster, Save the Children International, NRC, and the Ministry of Health.
• Visual Documentation: Professional photography and short video documentation of rehabilitation sessions, mobile team outreach, and patient fittings at the prosthetics center, produced in compliance with ethical guidelines for conflict-setting documentation.
Donor Visibility
All project assets will carry donor branding in compliance with the donor's visibility requirements, including facility signage, documentation, and digital communications. A dedicated section of RHS's website will document the program's progress. RHS will ensure that the donor's contribution is accurately and prominently acknowledged in all external communications, with dedicated donor recognition at the program launch event, at the rehabilitation points and the central prosthetics center, and in all media releases covering program milestones.

title: Organizational Background
content:
Restoring Hope Society (RHS) is a Jordanian humanitarian organization established in 2024 by Royal directive of H.M. King Abdullah II of Jordan. RHS operates under a mandate to restore dignity, independence, and wellbeing to populations affected by conflict, displacement, and humanitarian crisis, with a particular focus on rehabilitation services, disability inclusion, and multidisciplinary care for vulnerable individuals in the Middle East and beyond. RHS is headquartered in Amman, Jordan, and operates active programming in Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, with programmatic development underway for Yemen and additional conflict-affected contexts.

## Vision, Mission, and Values
Dimension
Statement
Vision
A Middle East and North Africa where every conflict-affected individual has access to the dignified, multidisciplinary, high-quality rehabilitation services they need to rebuild their lives.
Mission
To design, fund, and deliver integrated rehabilitation and capacity building programs in humanitarian settings — anchored in clinical evidence, driven by local ownership, and sustained by institutional development — for individuals living with disability resulting from conflict, injury, and poverty.
Values
Clinical excellence, institutional sustainability, dignity-centred practice, local partnership, evidence-based programming, and the non-negotiable integration of physical, psychological, and nutritional care.

## The RHS Hub-and-Spoke Rehabilitation Model
RHS operates a hub-and-spoke operational architecture designed to balance international quality standards with local institutional ownership and long-term sustainability. The Amman Center of Excellence (CoE) will serve as the clinical quality assurance hub, hosting ISPO-certified P&O specialists, the technical supervision function for rehabilitation, P&O, and MHPSS service standards, and the remote support infrastructure for field operations. Spoke programs, currently operational in Gaza and Syria, with Sudan in the development phase, deliver direct in-country services, with local practitioners and partner institutions providing day-to-day clinical care under RHS's Head Office remote academic and quality-assurance oversight.
This model has several critical advantages for the Gaza context, specifically. It allows the intensive international clinical expertise of RHS's ISPO-certified specialists to be applied directly to clinical supervision and patient fitting, while day-to-day service delivery remains in the hands of Gaza-based teams working within the Ministry of Health framework. When the project ends, the local service infrastructure — the rehabilitation points, the central prosthetics center, the equipped and experienced field teams, and the beneficiary database and case management systems — remains fully operational and entirely locally owned.

## RHS Track Record and Operational Capacity
Despite being a relatively young organization, RHS has demonstrated its operational and technical capacity through a growing portfolio of rehabilitation programs across the region. Key organizational achievements relevant to this proposal include: the successful design and submission of a complete ISPO-aligned prosthetics curriculum through the Palestinian Ministry of Higher Education; the establishment of an academic partnership with the University of Jordan's Faculty of Rehabilitation Sciences; the successful delivery of a prosthetic components and equipment shipment to Gaza in June 2026 (demonstrating logistics capability under active conflict conditions); and the development of a comprehensive 2026–2028 Strategic Plan establishing clear growth trajectories across Gaza, Syria, Sudan, and Yemen.
RHS employs qualified humanitarian professionals across programs, finance, communications, and protection, with technical direction provided by internationally recognized P&O specialists. The organization maintains robust financial management, donor reporting, and compliance systems appropriate to its scale and programmatic ambitions.
